The VITAL trial examined the effects of 2,000 IU daily vitamin D supplementation on musculoskeletal outcomes in generally healthy adults, including men (≥50 years) and women (≥55 years) over 5.3 years (n = 25,871), while the DO-HEALTH trial studied women and men (≥70 years) over 3 years (n = 2,157).

It's crucial to note that in generally healthy and vitamin D-replete older adults not preselected for vitamin D deficiency or low bone mass or osteoporosis, 2,000 IU/day of vitamin D had no musculoskeletal health benefits. ## Key Results

Menaquinone-7 had no major effect on the progression of aortic valve calcification as assessed by computed tomography or echocardiography. High-dose menaquinone-7 was safe and well tolerated.

**Study Overview:**
The study was a three-year, double-blind, randomized clinical trial conducted in a single center in Calgary, Canada, from August 2013 to December 2017, including 311 community-dwelling healthy adults without osteoporosis, aged 55 to 70 years, with baseline levels of 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25[OH]D) of 30 to 125 nmol/L.

**Study Design:**
Participants received daily doses of vitamin D3 for 3 years at 400 IU (n = 109), 4000 IU (n = 100), or 10,000 IU (n = 102), with calcium supplementation provided to participants with dietary intake of less than 1200 mg per day.

**Primary Outcomes:**
The co-primary outcomes were total volumetric BMD at radius and tibia, assessed with high resolution peripheral quantitative computed tomography, and bone strength (failure load) at radius and tibia estimated by finite element analysis.

**Key Results:**
Of 311 participants who were randomized (53% men; mean age, 62.2 years), 287 (92%) completed the study. Based on the significantly lower radial BMD seen with both 4,000 and 10,000 IU, compared with 400 IU; the lower tibial BMD with 10,000 IU, compared with 400 IU; and the lack of a difference in bone strength at the radius and tibia, the findings do not support a benefit of high-dose vitamin D supplementation for bone health.

The study was published in JAMA in 2019, August;322(8): 736-745.

## Study Overview

This study, published in the New England Journal of Medicine on July 28, 2022, investigated whether supplemental vitamin D affects incident fractures in midlife and older adults. The research was an ancillary study of the Vitamin D and Omega-3 Trial (VITAL).

## Study Design

VITAL was a two-by-two factorial, randomized, controlled trial that investigated whether supplemental vitamin D3 (2000 IU per day), n-3 fatty acids (1 g per day), or both would prevent cancer and cardiovascular disease in men 50 years of age or older and women 55 years of age or older in the United States. Participants were not recruited on the basis of vitamin D deficiency, low bone mass, or osteoporosis.

## Key Findings

Among 25,871 participants (50.6% women and 20.2% Black), 1,991 incident fractures were confirmed in 1,551 participants over a median follow-up of 5.3 years. 

Supplemental vitamin D3, as compared with placebo, did not have a significant effect on total fractures, nonvertebral fractures, or hip fractures. There was no modification of the treatment effect according to baseline characteristics, including age, sex, race or ethnic group, body-mass index, or serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels.

**Title:** The effect of vitamin MK-7 on bone mineral density and microarchitecture in postmenopausal women with osteopenia, a 3-year randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial

**Journal:** Osteoporosis International

**Year:** 2021

**DOI:** 10.1007/s00198-020-05638-z

## Abstract Summary

**Study Design:** A double-blinded, randomized controlled trial spanning three years

**Participants:** 142 postmenopausal women diagnosed with osteopenia

**Intervention:** Participants received either vitamin K2 (375 μg MK-7 daily) or placebo, with both groups also receiving vitamin D3 (38 μg/day) and calcium (800 mg/day)

**Key Results:** 
- Undercarboxylated osteocalcin showed significant reduction in the MK-7 group after one year
- After three years, bone mineral density "decreased at all sites without differences between the MK-7 and placebo-treated women"
- Changes in bone turnover markers and microstructure were comparable between groups
- The researchers concluded that while MK-7 enhanced osteocalcin carboxylation, it "did not affect biochemical markers of bone turnover, bone mineral density, or bone microarchitecture" over the full study period
